overview: East Strand is Portrush's long town beach, around 2.5km of sand running east from the promenade until it merges with Curran Strand and finally Whiterocks. Behind it sits a big dune system that holds the Royal Portrush golf links, and out to sea you look across to the Skerries and the Causeway headlands. On the grass bank by the beach is Holger Lonze's sculpture 'To the People of the Sea', a tribute to local boatbuilder James Kelly.

For surfing it is the most practical beach on the north coast. The council describes it as busy with watersports all year round, surfing above all, and the RNLI says surfers of every level use it. You get a large charged car park, toilets, cold outdoor showers and ramps onto the sand at both ends of the promenade, with the town's cafés and the railway station a short walk away.

Because the beach is so long you can usually walk away from the crowd near the town end. It is also popular with racehorse trainers, who exercise horses between Whiterocks and East Strand, so keep an eye out early and late in the day. Look out for gannets, eider, guillemots and terns offshore, and expect the beach to fill up quickly on warm summer weekends.

text: East Strand is an exposed sandy beach break with peaks going both left and right. Forecast sites rate the Portrush area best on a north-westerly groundswell with offshore winds from the south. Summer is often flat or small, while autumn through to spring brings more consistent swell. Banks shift with storms, so the best spot along the beach changes from week to week.

The RNLI has reported lifeguards rescuing a bodyboarder caught in a flash rip here, so check with the lifeguards before you paddle out and stay inside the flagged zones when they are on duty. Further east the beach gets more exposed, and Whiterocks at the far end usually picks up a little more swell.

When it's on, East Strand is a fast, hollow beach break that throws up punchy A-frame peaks over sand, with both lefts and rights. It likes a north-westerly swell, from around waist-high up to well overhead (roughly 3 to 15ft), and a southerly to south-easterly wind grooms it. It is surfable at every stage of the tide, with a rising tide from mid to high often the pick, and the wave shape holds fairly steady through the cycle.

This is the Causeway Coast's most consistent surf, so it fills up when it's good, and the paddle-out gets punishing and the rips run through the lineup as the swell builds. Winter is the best season, with January the cleanest month in forecast data, and summer is mostly flat. The water is cold, around 14°C, so bring a proper wetsuit, hood and boots. The surf shops in town, such as Troggs, are the people to ask about what it's doing today.

cards.label: Level
cards.title: Improvers and up
cards.text: Gentle days suit a lesson; beginners should go with a school and stay inside the flags.

cards.label: Conditions
cards.title: NW swell, southerly wind
cards.text: Works at all tides, mid to high on the rise is often best.

cards.label: Season
cards.title: Autumn to spring
cards.text: Winter is cleanest; summer is mostly flat and the water stays cold.

cards.label: Hazards
cards.title: Flash rips
cards.text: The RNLI has reported rescues from flash rips. Watch for horses and other water users too.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Large charged car park
practical.text: About 637 spaces, charged daily. Concrete ramps lead onto the sand at both ends of the promenade.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: Toilets and showers
practical.text: Toilets (including at the Watersports Centre), accessible toilets and parking, and outdoor cold showers. Beach access equipment can be pre-booked through the Mae Murray Foundation.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Seasonal RNLI patrol
practical.text: In 2026 the RNLI patrolled 10am–6pm over the Easter holidays, at weekends from mid-April to late June, daily from 27 June to 31 August and at weekends through September. No flags means no lifeguards.

practical.label: Dogs & horses
practical.title: Summer restrictions
practical.text: The council allows dogs but applies restrictions from 1 June to 15 September — check the signs at the entrance for where they apply. From 1 May to 30 September horse riding is only allowed before 11am and after 7pm.

practical.label: Getting here
practical.title: Train and town
practical.text: Portrush station is in the town, a short walk from the beach.

faqs.q: Is Portrush East Strand good for beginners?
faqs.a: Yes, on small days and inside the flagged zone when lifeguards are on duty. If you are new, take a lesson rather than going out alone.
In 2026 the RNLI patrolled daily from 27 June to 31 August, 10am–6pm, plus Easter, spring weekends and September weekends. Check the RNLI page for this year.
Yes, but the council applies restrictions from 1 June to 15 September.
Yes — the sand runs continuously east via Curran Strand to Whiterocks.

faqs.q: What tide is best at Portrush East Strand?
faqs.a: It's surfable at all stages. A rising tide from mid to high is often best, and the wave shape stays fairly steady through the cycle.
